summary: Comments by two early network people on the mail protocol proposed in RFC 524. They call it very rich but point out minor and major problems, such as the use of the Telnet Go-Ahead signal by a higher-level protocol and what the default signature should be. They also suggest that senders be able to give mail a priority.

eli5.summary: Some friends read a plan for how to send letters between computers. They said it was a good plan, listed a few things to fix, and suggested marking urgent letters.

questions: what was wrong with the rfc 524 mail protocol
why not make mail a subsystem of ftp
subtitle: Crocker and Postel review the mail protocol proposed in RFC 524, with minor and major objections.

tldr.problem: RFC 524 proposed a mail protocol, and the authors felt it was extremely rich but had some minor and some major problems.
tldr.mechanism: The note lists twelve minor points, such as priority levels and the order of parameters, and two larger issues about how the protocol relates to FTP and about forwarding.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of review comments and suggestions, not a protocol specification.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 539 as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It comments on RFC 524, and RFC 555 replies to these comments.

sections.title: Minor Points
sections.content:
The authors open by saying the protocol is extremely rich. Their minor points include explaining <CA> and <CA2> before the formal syntax, and making the default SIGNATURE the sign-on or ident of the author. They object to <CA2> because it is the Telnet Go-Ahead, which should not be used by higher level protocols.

They also ask that the ID command be clarified, that the formal syntax show the Static and Dynamic attribute distinction, that the document take a negative attitude toward requiring a login before accepting mail, and that cryptic default phrases such as "Author to the Clerk" be made clearer.
sections.eli5: First they listed small fixes, like explaining odd words earlier and using the writer's name as the default signature.

sections.title: Priority, Size and Parameter Order
sections.content:
The authors suggest that the INTERRUPT disposition carry author-assigned levels, for example 1 to 10, with no precisely defined meaning, and that the word be changed to URGENT or PRIORITY. A user could then ask to be told at once about Priority 5 or higher Short mail, or any Priority 10 mail.

They also want senders to be able to warn of the mail size, with a byte count and/or an imprecise SHORT/MEDIUM/LONG. Finally, they argue that requiring Static, Dynamic, then Optional parameters forces receivers to buffer before they can accept the mail, and propose the order Dynamic, Optional, Static so that mail can be rerouted by Priority and Length.
sections.eli5: They wanted a way to say how urgent and how long a letter is, and to send that information first so the receiver can decide early.

sections.title: FTP and Rerouting
sections.content:
The larger issues start with a strong statement in favor of unified access, with one selector process and one listening socket. Since that does not exist yet, they argue the Mail Protocol should not be a subsystem of FTP. It should use FTP the way RJE does, which raises the issue of logging in to send mail.

They also suggest a way to reroute mail just before it is received, so a host can refuse a piece of mail but name an alternate receiver. Three variations are described: automatic forwarding, automatic forwarding with a copy held, and rerouting without accepting. The last needs a special reply code, 476 <recipient> IS AT <pathname>, given in reply to a RECIPIENT command.
sections.eli5: They said mail should borrow the file-sending system but not live inside it, and that a computer should be able to say "this person's mail goes over there instead."

references.text: RFC 524, the mail protocol proposal being reviewed.
